title: Every Friday
hook: every Friday is a small day of penance, meat or another sacrifice by local rule

segments.voice: Yesterday, the months have themes, a quieter calendar under the feasts. Your line was every month a door. What sign did you put out? Day six hundred ninety.

Why does a fast-food chain famous for burgers sell a fish sandwich? The story told in the business world is that a franchise owner in a heavily Catholic part of Cincinnati, around 1962, was losing money every Friday because his customers wouldn't eat meat that day. So he invented a fish sandwich, and it went national. Whether every detail is true, the pattern behind it certainly is: for centuries, on Fridays, Catholics simply didn't eat meat. Many still don't. And the reason sits underneath every week of the year.
screen: `A FISH SANDWICH IN CINCINNATI.` → `NO MEAT ON FRIDAYS.` → `A REASON UNDER EVERY WEEK.`

segments.voice: The word is abstinence, from the Latin abstinere, to hold back. In Church law it means a specific thing: not eating meat. Fasting is different; fasting means eating less, one full meal. Catholics fast and abstain on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and abstain on the Fridays of Lent. But the Church's law goes further than Lent. Canon law says that every Friday of the year is a day of penance, because Friday is the day Jesus died. Every Friday is a small Good Friday. The law names abstinence from meat as the usual way to keep it, from age fourteen, unless a solemnity falls on that Friday. And it lets each country's bishops set the details. That's where it gets local. In the United States since 1966, outside of Lent, the bishops allow Catholics to choose another penance instead: an act of charity, extra prayer, giving up something else. In England and Wales, the bishops brought back the meat rule in 2011. So a Catholic in London and one in Chicago may keep Friday differently, and both are keeping the law. Why meat and not, say, bread? Historically, meat was the festive food, the expensive one; fish was the ordinary food of the poor. The point was never that meat is bad. It's a small, regular no that makes room for a larger yes. Jesus put it this way, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily."
screen: `ABSTINERE: TO HOLD BACK.` · `EVERY FRIDAY A DAY OF PENANCE.` · `LOCAL RULES: US AND ENGLAND.` · `A SMALL NO FOR A LARGER YES.` · then, large: `LET HIM DENY HIMSELF, AND TAKE UP HIS CROSS DAILY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a Friday sacrifice. Sit, and think about your ordinary Friday. What's one thing you could quietly go without, or add, every Friday for the next month? Meat is the classic. It could also be your phone at lunch, dessert, a drive you could walk, or an hour of time given to someone else. Choose something small enough to keep. If you pray, you can offer it for someone. If you don't, simply notice how holding back feels. The bell holds the time.
Abstinence. From the Latin for holding back: in Church law, going without meat, the usual Friday penance, with local rules about substitutes. Today's word.
Your line: every friday a little lent. This Friday, keep the sacrifice you chose, and remember why the day was chosen. Day six hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Catholic canon law makes every Friday a day of penance; many Catholics abstain from meat on all Fridays, and where bishops permit, as in the United States outside Lent, others choose a different penance such as charity or prayer.
